processing: The leaf is versatile: locally it has gone into sun-dried tea, pan-fired and baked greens, and black tea. As a white tea it follows the usual class method of withering and drying, without a kill-green or rolling.
harvest_season: Spring is best, above all before Qingming; the autumn 'rice-flower' picking ranks lower.
appearance_dry: Fat, heavy, densely downy shoots with silvery white hair.
appearance_liquor: Clear and bright; pale yellow in white-style tea.
appearance_wet: Thick, large buds and leaves, soft and downy.
taste_profile: Clean fragrance and a mellow body that turns sweet in the aftertaste, and it stands up to repeated steeping.

brewing.notes: Plump buds open slowly, so start with a longer first steep than you would give small-leaf white tea. This is general guidance for large-bud white tea.

vintage_note: Spring lots carry the premium, with pre-Qingming pickings at the top, and autumn pickings sit below them. As with other Yunnan whites, expect the harvest year on the label and both fresh and stored tea on sale, so check which you are buying.
description:
Yangta Dabai comes from Yangta village in Minle, Jinggu county, in misty high country in Yunnan. What sets it apart is the plant: a large-leaf local type whose shoots are so thickly covered in down that the finished tea looks strikingly white.

That leaf is not tied to one tea type. Local makers have used it for sun-dried tea, for pan-fired and baked greens, and for black tea with visible golden tips. Makers near Jinggu also pulled the leaf into straight strands and sold it in bundles known as ba ba cha.

Expect a clean fragrance, a mellow body and a returning sweetness, with enough stamina for several steeps. Do not rush it: big buds give up their flavour slowly, and a short first steep tastes thin.

Buy by season. Spring tea is favoured and pre-Qingming is the top lot, while autumn tea ranks below. Because this leaf can be made in several ways, confirm what style you are getting before you judge it, since a Yangta green and a Yangta white have little in common in the cup.
history:
Local accounts put the planting in Yangta at around 1840 and say old mother trees still stand, though the figures given for the tea's age vary between about 140 and 160 years. Those accounts also say a local official, struck by how white the leaf looked, ordered it carefully made as a tribute tea called Bai Long Xu, white dragon whiskers. This comes from regional write-ups rather than court records.

The later dates are more concrete: Yangta Dabai is reported as named one of Yunnan's eight famous teas in 1981, and as included in the tea volume of the Encyclopedia of Chinese Agriculture published in 1989.
